captions: Part six.
The modern era.
For nearly a decade,

convolution was the undisputed king of
vision.
Then an idea,
born over in the world of language models,
crossed over — and shook everything up all
over again.
That idea is attention.
Let's watch how it learned to see.
This is the Vision Transformer,
usually shortened to ViT.
And its core idea is delightfully strange.
Treat an image exactly like a sentence.
Let's see how.
First,
we cut the image up into a grid
of small square patches — say,
sixteen pixels by sixteen pixels each.
Watch the patches lift off the image and
line up in a single row.
Each patch now becomes a token — the
very same concept as a word in a
sentence.
So an image becomes a sentence of patches.
Then we feed that row of tokens into

a standard transformer — the exact same
architecture

that powers large language models like the
one
you may have chatted with.

The transformer's key mechanism is
self-attention.
Here is what it does.
Every patch looks at every other patch,
and decides which ones are relevant to it.
Look at the arcs connecting the patches —
a patch of ear reaching across to a
patch of eye,
linking distant parts of the image in a
single step.
And this is the crucial difference from a
C N N.
A convolution only ever sees a small local
window,
and has to build up a global view
slowly,
layer by layer.

A transformer sees the entire image at
once,
from its very first layer.
There is a catch,
and it is worth knowing.
ViT is hungry.
It needs a lot of data to learn
well,
more than a C N N does.
But give it that data,

and it matches or beats convolution
outright.
And the best part — if you already
understand attention from language models,
then you already understand ViT.

The tokens are just patches instead of
words.
